questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a parameter from a statistic
questions.stem: Dashboard note 1: the mean response time of all 10,000 users in the population is 240 ms; a sample of 50 users has mean 232 ms. Which value is the parameter?

options.text: 240 ms, because it describes the entire population.
232 ms, because it comes from observed data.
The difference 8 ms, because it measures bias.
options.misconception: treats a difference as a parameter

options.text: 50, because it is the sample size.
options.misconception: confuses sample size with a parameter

questions.explanation: A parameter describes the population; 240 ms is the population mean. The sample mean 232 ms is a statistic. The difference and sample size are neither.
questions.hint: Parameter describes the population, statistic the sample.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.stem: Dashboard note 2: an analyst uses the sample range as an estimate of the population range. What is the main issue?

options.text: The sample range is unbiased for any sample size.
options.misconception: assumes range is an unbiased estimator

options.text: The sample range is biased downward and underestimates the population range.
The sample range overestimates because outliers are common.
Range is not a statistic and cannot be computed.
options.misconception: thinks range is not a computable statistic

questions.explanation: The sample range tends to be smaller than the population range, so it is biased downward. Bias is a systematic error, not random variation.
questions.hint: Sample extremes rarely reach population extremes.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State conditions for a sampling distribution
questions.stem: Dashboard note 3: which condition is required for the sampling distribution of the sample mean to be approximately normal?

options.text: The sample size must be at least 1000 for any population.
The population must be exactly normal regardless of sample size.
The sample is random and either the population is normal or n is large enough.
The observations must be paired.

questions.explanation: Random sampling plus either population normality or large n (CLT) gives approximate normality. Exact normality and pairing are not required.
questions.hint: Random sample plus normality or large n.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.stem: Dashboard note 4: population mean 50, population sd 12, sample size 36. What is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean?
questions.explanation: Standard error = sigma/sqrt(n) = 12/sqrt(36) = 12/6 = 2.
questions.hint: Divide the population sd by the square root of n.

options.text: There is a 95% probability the true mean lies in this one interval.
95% of the sample data lie inside the interval.
options.misconception: confuses data coverage with interval coverage

options.text: About 95% of intervals from repeated sampling would contain the true mean.

questions.explanation: The confidence level describes the long-run capture rate of the method, not the probability for a single interval or the data spread.
questions.hint: Confidence level is about repeated intervals.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The null hypothesis as a reference
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the null hypothesis
questions.stem: Dashboard note 6: why is the null hypothesis described as a reference value in a significance test?

answer.exemplar: The null supplies a specific parameter value so the sampling distribution of the test statistic can be computed and a p-value obtained.

questions.explanation: Without a specified null value, there is no reference distribution for the test statistic. The null fixes the centre of the sampling distribution.
questions.hint: The null fixes the centre of the reference distribution.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.stem: Dashboard note 7: a test reports p = 0.03. Which statement is correct?

options.text: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true.
options.misconception: treats p-value as probability of the null

options.text: If the null were true, the chance of a result at least this extreme is about 0.03.
There is a 97% chance the alternative is true.
The effect size is 3% of the maximum possible.

questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme under the null, not the probability the null is true or an effect size.
questions.hint: p-value is about data under the null.

Type II error, a false negative.
options.misconception: confuses Type I and Type II

options.text: Type I error, a false positive.

questions.explanation: Rejecting a true null is a Type I error (false positive). A Type II error is failing to reject a false null.

questions.stem: Dashboard note 9: what is statistical power and why does increasing sample size increase it?

answer.exemplar: Power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null; larger n shrinks the standard error, making true effects easier to detect.

questions.explanation: Power is the chance of detecting an effect when it exists. Larger samples reduce variability, sharpening the test and raising power.
questions.hint: Power is detection probability; larger n reduces variability.

questions.stem: Dashboard note 45: after computing a 99% CI, an analyst says 'there is a 99% chance the true mean is in this interval.' What is wrong?

options.text: The interval should be a prediction interval instead.
Nothing is wrong; that is the correct interpretation.
The probability should be 95%, not 99%.
options.misconception: quibbles over the level rather than the concept

options.text: The true mean is fixed; the interval either contains it or not. The 99% refers to the method's long-run rate.

questions.explanation: The parameter is fixed and the interval is random before sampling. The confidence level describes the method's long-run capture rate, not a probability for one interval.
questions.hint: The parameter is fixed, not random.

questions.topic: The null hypothesis as a reference
questions.stem: Dashboard note 46: test whether mean latency differs from 200 ms. What is the null hypothesis?

options.text: H0: mu = 200 ms.
H0: xbar = 200 ms.
options.misconception: uses sample mean instead of population mean

options.text: H0: sigma = 200 ms.

questions.explanation: The null states the parameter equals the reference value: mu = 200 ms. The alternative is inequality, and xbar or sigma are not the parameter.
questions.hint: Null states parameter equals reference value.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.stem: Dashboard note 47: Test A p = 0.02, Test B p = 0.001, same null and sample size. Which provides stronger evidence against the null?

options.text: They are equal because both are significant.
options.misconception: thinks any significant p implies equal evidence

options.text: Test A, because a larger p-value is more credible.
Test B, because the smaller p-value indicates stronger evidence against the null.
Neither, because p-values cannot be compared.

questions.explanation: With the same design, a smaller p-value indicates stronger evidence against the null. Both are significant but not equally strong.
questions.hint: Smaller p means stronger evidence.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II errors
questions.stem: Dashboard note 48: a test fails to reject a false null hypothesis. What error occurred?

options.text: A confidence error.
Type I error, a false positive.
options.misconception: confuses Type I and Type II

options.text: A power error.
Type II error, a false negative.

questions.explanation: Failing to reject a false null is a Type II error (false negative). A Type I error is rejecting a true null.

questions.learningObjective: State an assumption of the F test
questions.stem: Dashboard note 52: which assumption is most critical for an F test comparing two variances?

options.text: The data must be paired.
The sample sizes must be equal.
The means must be equal.
Both populations should be approximately normal.

questions.explanation: The F test for variances is sensitive to non-normality, so approximate normality is critical. Equal n, equal means, and pairing are not required.
questions.hint: Normality is the key assumption.

questions.stem: Dashboard note 56: an analyst runs a two-tailed test, gets p = 0.08, then reports a one-tailed p = 0.04 and claims significance. Identify the error.

options.text: One-tailed tests are never allowed.
The one-tailed p-value should be 0.16, not 0.04.
The tail was chosen after seeing the data, inflating Type I error.
The error is using 0.05 instead of 0.01.

questions.explanation: Choosing the tail after seeing the data is invalid and inflates Type I error. A one-tailed test must be pre-specified.
